newsitem.title: USA: GFOA says excluded from litigation reform hearing.
newsitem.headline: GFOA says excluded from litigation reform hearing.

text.p: States and localities are not getting their fair chance to warn a Senate panel about the impact Congress' 1995 securities litigation reforms have had on municipalities, a group said Wednesday.

The Government Finance Officers Association on Wednesday lashed out at the two top members of Senate Banking Committee's Securities Subommittee for excluding states and localities from testifying before the committee as lawmakers are weighing whether more reforms are needed.

"It is difficult to understand why the Subcommittee was unable to find the time to hear from a single yet significant witness representing state and local government market participants," the association wrote to Committee chairman Phil Gramm, a Texas Republican, and ranking Democrat Chris Dodd, of Connecticut.

The state and local group's comments come a day before Gramm's panel will hear the views of the securities industry, technology companies and others who are seeking even more changes to keep what they call meritless cases from migrating to state courts.

A committee aide said the state and local group, among others, would be able to testify before the panel if legislation were introduced to mirror a House bill that would restrict securities class actions from being tried in state courts.
Sources familiar with the matter say Gramm and Dodd will likely introduce such legislation in the fall.
In 1995, Congress enacted the reforms, over President Clinton's veto, which aim to reduce the amount of meritless securities class actions that find their way into federal courts.
Consumer advocates, including state and local government representatives, say the reforms have left investors with little protection and are now warning against setting more curbs.

The Uniform Standards Coalition, a nationwide organization of high-tech companies and venture capitalists, has been urging lawmakers and even White House officials, that more reforms are needed. The powerful group claims that litigators have been able to get around the 1995 reforms by moving securities class actions to state courts.
More reforms would be good news for the Securities Industry Association, which also maintains that trial lawyers have found a loophole in the 1995 reforms by moving cases to state courts.

"This problem needs to be addressed before real harm is done to our markets," Joseph Pollizzotto, managing director at Lehman Brothers, said in his prepared testimony to be given at the Thursday hearing. "This loophole may become a noose around the necks of high tech firms and other legitimate market participants unless Congress steps in to cut the rope."

Securities and Exchange Commission Chairman Arthur Levitt will also testify, but sources familiar with the issue say he will likely maintain his stance that it is too soon to tell whether or not more reforms are needed.
Clinton Administration officials separately have been actively reviewing the issue, sources close to the matter say.
